explanation: Loose joints take months to tighten up, and bending over a baby strains an already vulnerable back. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h6)

question: Numbness and tingling in the fingers during pregnancy are classic signs of what condition?
explanation: Fluid retention in the wrist compresses the median nerve, causing tingling and numbness in the hand. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h7)

question: A pregnant woman complains of severe lower back pain and an unstable pelvis. What nursing advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Take high-dose calcium tablets and complete strict bed rest
options.B: Apply ice packs directly to the lower spine for six hours daily
options.C: Avoid walking entirely until after the baby is safely delivered
options.D: Wear a supportive pelvic belt and practice safe body mechanics

explanation: Support belts help stabilize loose pelvic joints, and proper body mechanics protect the spine from further strain. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T8#GNS121_U7_T8_h7)

question: Which hormone is primarily responsible for increased melanin production during pregnancy?
explanation: Elevated levels of melanocyte-stimulating hormone directly activate melanocytes to produce more pigment during gestation. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h1)

question: Oestrogen contributes to pregnancy-related skin changes by causing what effect?

options.A: Increased dermal blood flow and vascular permeability
options.B: Complete cessation of sweat gland secretions
options.C: Rapid destruction of subcutaneous fat layers
options.D: Decreased production of natural skin oils

explanation: Higher oestrogen levels expand blood vessels in the skin, leading to increased warmth and visible vascular markings. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h1)

question: What is the dark midline vertical line on the pregnant abdomen called?
explanation: Linea nigra is the pigmented line that commonly develops down the center of the abdomen during pregnancy. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h2)

question: Melasma during pregnancy typically presents in which pattern on the face?

options.A: Scattered white depigmented spots on the eyelids
options.B: Bright red circular rings across the chin
options.C: Irregular brown patches on the forehead and cheeks
options.D: Painful fluid-filled blisters around the lips

explanation: Melasma creates dark, blotchy patches symmetrically distributed over sun-exposed areas of the face like cheeks and forehead. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h2)

question: Striae gravidarum on the abdomen are primarily caused by stretching and changes in what skin component?
explanation: Hormonal shifts alter collagen and elastin fibers, which tear under mechanical tension to form striae gravidarum. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h3)

question: Spider angiomas develop during pregnancy due to which physiological factor?

options.A: Increased platelet aggregation in superficial skin layers
options.B: Blocked lymphatic drainage in the upper extremities
options.C: High levels of circulating oestrogen dilating small blood vessels
options.D: Reduced blood volume causing localized tissue hypoxia

explanation: Elevated oestrogen triggers the dilation of superficial capillaries, creating the characteristic spider-like vascular lesions. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h3)

question: Why do many pregnant women experience thicker hair during gestation?

options.A: Hormones prolong the growth phase of hair follicles
options.B: Blood flow to hair roots decreases significantly
options.C: Protein intake is automatically stored in hair shafts
options.D: Sebum production increases along the scalp

explanation: Pregnancy hormones keep hair in the growing phase longer, delaying the normal shedding process. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h4)

question: What happens to a woman's hair shortly after childbirth?

options.A: Individual hair strands become thicker and coarser
options.B: Hair color permanently changes to a lighter shade
options.C: Mass shedding occurs as follicles enter the resting phase
options.D: Hair growth stops completely for at least one year

explanation: Postpartum hormone drops cause delayed shedding to happen all at once, known as telogen effluvium. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h4)

question: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is characterized by severe itching most notably on which body parts?
explanation: Bile acid accumulation in cholestasis causes intense pruritus that classically affects the palms and soles first. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h5)

question: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy most commonly first appear in which location?

options.B: On the soles of the feet

explanation: These itchy bumps usually originate within the striae gravidarum on the abdomen before spreading. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h5)

question: What is a common immediate skin response observed during active labour?
explanation: High physical exertion and metabolic activity during labour trigger heavy diaphoresis. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h6)

question: How do striae gravidarum typically change months after childbirth?

options.A: They expand and develop fluid-filled blisters
options.B: They fade into silvery-white, less prominent scars
options.C: They disappear completely without a trace
options.D: They turn into dark brown raised nodules

explanation: Although stretch marks remain permanent, their color softens from red-purple to a silvery-white hue over time. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h6)

question: Which symptom reported by a pregnant woman requires immediate medical reporting due to potential foetal risk?

options.A: Severe generalized itching without an obvious rash
options.B: Gradual darkening of the linea nigra on the abdomen
options.C: Softening and mild brittleness of the fingernails
options.D: Development of small spider angiomas on the cheeks

explanation: Generalized pruritus points toward intrahepatic cholestasis, which demands prompt medical evaluation for foetal safety. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h7)

question: What is a primary goal of nursing education regarding normal dermatological changes in pregnancy?

options.A: Prescribing topical steroid creams for every reported skin lesion
options.B: Reassuring mothers about benign changes while teaching warning signs
options.C: Encouraging surgical removal of vascular markings before delivery
options.D: Preventing all forms of hormonal hyperpigmentation with strict diets

explanation: Nurses help alleviate anxiety by explaining normal pigment shifts while ensuring dangerous conditions are identified early. [learn more](GNS121_U7_T9#GNS121_U7_T9_h7)

question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Exocrine glands have no connection to epithelial surfaces.
options.B: Endocrine glands rely exclusively on ducts to release secretions.
options.C: Exocrine glands produce hormones instead of enzymes.
options.D: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.

explanation: Ductless endocrine glands release their chemical messengers straight into capillaries, whereas exocrine glands use ducts to empty substances onto surfaces. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do endocrine responses usually take longer than nervous system responses?

options.A: Nerves use chemical neurotransmitters instead of electrical impulses.
options.B: Hormones require direct contact with target cell surface proteins.
options.C: Endocrine organs process stimuli much slower than spinal nerves.
options.D: Hormones must travel through the circulatory system to reach targets.

explanation: Circulating blood carries hormones across the body, which takes more time than electrical signals moving along a nerve cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which structure connects the nervous system to the endocrine system?
explanation: The hypothalamus receives signals from the brain and turns them into hormonal messages to control the pituitary gland. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which hormones are stored and released by the posterior pituitary gland?
explanation: Special cells in the hypothalamus make oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone, and send them down to be stored in the posterior pituitary. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which dietary element is needed to make thyroid hormones?
explanation: The thyroid gland needs iodine to build working thyroxine and triiodothyronine molecules. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is the main job of parathyroid hormone?

options.C: To promote sodium and water excretion

explanation: Parathyroid hormone acts on bones, kidneys, and the gut to bring calcium levels back up when they drop too low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which hormone is the main mineralocorticoid released by the adrenal cortex?
explanation: Aldosterone helps balance electrolytes by telling the kidneys to hold onto sodium and get rid of potassium. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: How does the adrenal medulla work differently from the adrenal cortex?

options.A: The medulla responds rapidly to acute stress through neural stimulation.
options.B: The medulla secretes steroid hormones necessary for long-term survival.
options.C: The medulla relies entirely on anterior pituitary tropic signals.
options.D: The medulla regulates serum calcium instead of blood glucose.

explanation: Nerves from the sympathetic nervous system connect directly to the adrenal medulla to trigger an instant release of stress hormones like adrenaline. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which specific cells in the pancreas make insulin?
explanation: Insulin is produced and released by the beta cells found inside the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the main action of glucagon in the body?

options.A: To increase blood glucose by breaking down stored glycogen
options.B: To suppress the production of digestive enzymes in the gut
options.C: To promote cellular glucose uptake in skeletal muscles
options.D: To stimulate fat storage in adipose tissue depots

explanation: Glucagon tells the liver to break down stored sugar (glycogen) and release it into the blood when blood sugar levels are low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which hormone does the pineal gland release to help control sleep cycles?
explanation: The pineal gland makes more melatonin when it gets dark outside, signaling to the body that it is time to sleep. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the main job of Leydig cells in the male reproductive system?
explanation: Leydig cells inside the testes make and release testosterone when signaled by luteinizing hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: How does a negative feedback loop work in the endocrine system?

options.A: It continuously increases hormone production until medical intervention occurs.
options.B: It suppresses further hormone release when target levels become too high.
options.C: It speeds up metabolic pathways regardless of circulating hormone concentrations.
options.D: It reverses nervous system signals without involving chemical messengers.

explanation: Negative feedback acts like a thermostat, slowing down hormone production once levels reach the right amount. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)

question: Which situation is an example of a positive feedback mechanism in the body?

options.A: Insulin lowering blood glucose levels after a carbohydrate-rich meal
options.B: Aldosterone causing renal sodium reabsorption to raise blood pressure
options.C: Oxytocin release intensifying uterine contractions during labor
options.D: Thyroid hormone suppressing thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion

explanation: Childbirth uses positive feedback because the stretching of the cervix causes more oxytocin to be released, which makes contractions even stronger. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)

question: What structure carries endocrine hormones directly to target organs?
explanation: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood circulation to reach distant target tissues. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: Why do only specific cells respond to a circulating hormone?

options.A: Target cells are located closer to glands

explanation: Cells must express the correct receptor protein to bind and respond to a specific chemical messenger. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h1)

question: What is the primary chemical precursor for steroid hormones?
explanation: All steroid hormones are synthesized from cholesterol within endocrine tissues like the adrenal cortex and gonads. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: What determines how a hormone is transported in the blood?

options.B: The size of the target organ
options.D: The time of day it is released

explanation: Water-soluble hormones dissolve freely in plasma, whereas lipid-soluble hormones require carrier proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which amino acid serves as the precursor for catecholamines?
explanation: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine are all synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: How do thyroid hormones differ chemically from typical amine hormones?

options.A: They are lipid-soluble despite being amino acid derivatives
options.B: They are synthesized as large proteins and broken down
options.C: They are stored in large amounts in the bloodstream
options.D: They do not require receptors to enter target cells

explanation: Unlike most amino acid derivatives that are water-soluble, thyroid hormones incorporate iodine and act like lipid-soluble steroids. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the primary solubility characteristic of peptide hormones?
explanation: Peptide hormones dissolve readily in water and blood plasma without needing specialized transport proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Why must peptide hormones bind to surface membrane receptors?

options.A: They require carrier proteins inside the cytoplasm
options.B: They degrade immediately upon touching cell surfaces
options.C: They cannot cross the lipid bilayer of the cell
options.D: They are too small to trigger intracellular enzymes

explanation: Hydrophilic peptide hormones are blocked by the hydrophobic interior of the cell membrane, requiring external receptors. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h4)

question: Which of the following is classified as a steroid hormone?
explanation: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid steroid hormone produced by the adrenal cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: What challenge do steroid hormones face when traveling in the blood?

options.A: They do not mix well with watery blood plasma
options.B: They precipitate out as solid crystals
options.C: They bind prematurely to red blood cells
options.D: They are rapidly destroyed by circulating enzymes

explanation: Being hydrophobic, steroid hormones must bind to plasma carrier proteins to remain suspended in circulation. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the main advantage of carrier proteins for lipid-soluble hormones?

options.A: They prolong the hormone half-life in blood
options.B: They actively push hormones into target cells
options.C: They convert lipid hormones into peptides
options.D: They accelerate the destruction of hormones

explanation: Carrier proteins shield lipid-soluble hormones from rapid breakdown by liver and kidney enzymes. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which fraction of a lipid-soluble hormone is biologically active in the blood?

options.D: The portion stored in fat tissue

explanation: Only hormones that are not bound to carrier proteins can leave the capillary and interact with target tissues. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h6)

question: Where are receptors for lipid-soluble hormones typically located?

options.C: On the outer cell membrane surface
options.D: Floating freely in the blood plasma

explanation: Lipid-soluble hormones easily cross the cell membrane to bind intracellular receptors inside the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)

question: How do water-soluble hormones usually exert their effects on target cells?

options.A: By using second messenger systems inside the cell
options.B: By dissolving the cell membrane to enter cytoplasm
options.C: By binding directly to DNA strands in the nucleus
options.D: By converting directly into intracellular enzymes

explanation: Surface binding triggers intracellular signaling cascades, or second messengers, since the hormone cannot enter the cell itself. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T10#GNS211_U1_T10_h7)

question: Where are intracellular receptors primarily located within a target cell?
explanation: Lipid-soluble steroid hormones cross the cell membrane easily to bind receptors residing inside the cytoplasm or nucleus. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h1)

question: What is the primary role of hormone receptors during cellular signaling?

options.A: Translating chemical messages into intracellular action
options.B: Destroying unwanted proteins inside the cytoplasm
options.C: Transporting nutrients across the plasma membrane
options.D: Producing excess circulating hormones in the blood

explanation: Receptors recognize specific circulating hormones and convert that binding event into an internal cellular response. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h1)

question: What happens during the process of receptor downregulation?

options.A: Cells increase their hormone production rate
options.B: Hormones bind permanently to cell walls
options.C: Receptors block all incoming blood flow
options.D: Cells decrease their total receptor number

explanation: Prolonged high hormone levels trigger cells to pull receptors inside and degrade them, lowering sensitivity. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h2)

question: A patient on long-term hormone therapy suddenly stops medication, experiencing deficiency symptoms because of what cellular process?
explanation: Long-term high drug exposure causes downregulation, leaving too few receptors to respond when therapy abruptly stops. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the effect of a constitutively active receptor mutation?

options.A: Immediate death of the target cell
options.C: Complete destruction of all circulating hormones

explanation: Constitutively active mutations lock the receptor into an 'on' state, driving cellular activity without any hormone present. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why might a patient show deficiency symptoms despite having high blood hormone levels?

options.A: Inactivating receptor mutations prevent tissue response
options.B: Red blood cells are carrying too much oxygen
options.C: The liver is destroying all circulating nutrients
options.D: The kidneys are excreting hormones too quickly

explanation: If receptors carry inactivating mutations, target tissues cannot detect the hormone regardless of how much circulates. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h3)

question: What does HER2 receptor amplification indicate in a breast cancer tumor sample?

options.A: Resistance to all known medical therapies
options.C: A low risk of disease recurrence

explanation: Overexpression or amplification of the HER2 protein drives rapid cell division, marking aggressive breast cancer subtypes. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why are breast tumors tested for estrogen and progesterone receptors?

options.B: To calculate the exact blood volume in the body
options.D: To measure the patient's daily fluid intake

explanation: Finding positive estrogen or progesterone receptors allows clinicians to prescribe specific hormone-blocking drugs that starve the tumor. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is the primary action of a pharmacological receptor antagonist?

options.A: Blocking natural hormones from binding the receptor
options.B: Mimicking the exact action of the natural hormone
options.C: Destroying the target cell through direct lysis
options.D: Increasing the synthesis of new hormone receptors

explanation: Antagonists occupy receptor sites without triggering activation, preventing the natural hormone from attaching. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h5)

question: How do monoclonal antibodies differ structurally from small molecule antagonists?

options.A: They act exclusively as permanent cellular agonists
options.B: They easily cross the nuclear membrane to bind DNA
options.C: They dissolve completely in the bloodstream without binding
options.D: They are large laboratory-made proteins targeting extracellular sites

explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are large protein structures tailored to attach to external cell-surface receptors like HER2. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h5)

question: How do cancer cells typically survive anti-hormone drug therapy over time?

options.A: By converting normal red blood cells into tumors
options.B: By slowing down their rate of blood circulation
options.C: By absorbing more vitamins from the bloodstream
options.D: By developing alternative survival pathways or receptor mutations

explanation: Tumors adapt to selective drug pressure by altering receptor structures or switching to different growth pathways. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the clinical outcome if a breast cancer tumor completely loses its estrogen receptors during treatment?

options.B: The tumor will shrink much faster than before
options.C: The patient requires higher doses of estrogen

explanation: Without estrogen receptors present, drugs designed to block those specific receptors no longer have a target to affect. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why must nurses monitor cardiac function in patients receiving certain HER2 inhibitors?

options.A: Chemotherapy causes immediate blood clots in the lungs
options.B: Patients naturally develop high blood pressure from age
options.C: The drug directly destroys heart valve tissue
options.D: HER2 pathways also play a role in myocardial protection

explanation: HER2 signaling is important for heart muscle health, making cardiac monitoring essential during targeted therapy. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h7)

question: Which diagnostic test is routinely required before and during HER2 inhibitor therapy?
explanation: Serial echocardiograms check left ventricular ejection fraction to catch early signs of cardiac dysfunction during treatment. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete directly into blood
options.B: Endocrine glands have special tubes for drainage
options.C: Exocrine glands rely on reticular fibers

explanation: Endocrine glands do not have ducts, so they release their chemical messengers straight into the surrounding fluid and blood vessels. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why are there so many tiny blood vessels around endocrine cells?

options.A: To give physical support to delicate cells
options.B: To filter out unwanted chemicals before they travel
options.C: To allow rapid movement of hormones directly into the blood
options.D: To keep harmful germs away from hormones

explanation: Having many small, porous blood vessels nearby ensures that hormones quickly enter the bloodstream to reach their target organs. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h1)

question: Where is the pituitary gland located in the skull?

options.A: Inside the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone
options.B: Attached to the back of the skull

explanation: The pituitary gland rests securely inside a small, bony depression called the sella turcica. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the main job of the hypophyseal portal system?

options.A: Carrying hormones to the rest of the body
options.C: Draining extra fluid away from the brain
options.D: Transporting hypothalamic signals to the anterior pituitary

explanation: Portal veins carry chemical signals directly from the hypothalamus to the front part of the pituitary gland without mixing into general circulation first. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the gel-like fluid inside thyroid follicles called?
explanation: Thyroid follicles store their hormone materials inside a thick, protein-rich fluid known as colloid. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which cells in the parathyroid glands make parathyroid hormone?
explanation: Chief cells are the primary cells responsible for making parathyroid hormone in the parathyroid glands. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which middle zone of the adrenal cortex produces cortisol?
explanation: The zona fasciculata is the wide middle layer of the adrenal cortex that makes cortisol. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: What type of cells make up the inner adrenal medulla?
explanation: Chromaffin cells are specialized cells that release adrenaline and noradrenaline directly into nearby blood sinuses. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h4)

question: Which cells in the pancreas produce insulin?
explanation: Beta cells are located in the center of the pancreatic islets and produce insulin to lower blood sugar. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the main job of alpha cells in the pancreas?

options.D: Releasing glucagon to raise blood sugar

explanation: Alpha cells release glucagon when blood sugar is low, telling the liver to release stored glucose. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h5)

question: What hormone is produced by the pineal gland?
explanation: Pineal cells produce melatonin, which helps regulate sleep-wake cycles and your internal body clock. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: Where is the thymus gland located during its active development?
explanation: The thymus sits in the upper chest area, just behind the sternum, during its active developmental phases. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which hormone is produced by the kidneys?
explanation: The kidneys release erythropoietin to signal the bone marrow to make more red blood cells when oxygen levels are low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is the main role of enteroendocrine cells in the gut?
explanation: Enteroendocrine cells release local hormones that control gut movement, digestive juices, and acid production. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h7)

question: What type of tiny blood vessels are usually found inside endocrine glands?
explanation: Fenestrated capillaries have tiny pores that let newly made hormones easily pass into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h8)

question: Which feature is NOT found in standard endocrine glands?

options.C: Cells arranged in cords or clumps

explanation: Endocrine glands do not have ducts; they are ductless organs that release their products straight into the blood. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T2#GNS211_U1_T2_h8)

question: What is the main job of the endocrine system in the human body?

options.C: Regulating body processes using chemical messengers

explanation: The endocrine system uses hormones released into the bloodstream to coordinate slow, steady body activities across different organs. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: How does endocrine signaling differ from nervous system signaling?

options.A: Nervous system responses last much longer than endocrine responses
options.B: Nervous signals target only the pancreas and adrenals
options.C: Endocrine communication needs direct cell-to-cell contact
options.D: Endocrine signals rely on hormones travelling through blood to produce slower effects

explanation: Hormones travel through the blood to reach distant cells, taking more time to work but lasting longer than fast nerve impulses. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h1)

question: Where are the receptors for steroid hormones usually found inside a cell?

options.C: Attached to the outer blood vessel walls
options.D: Embedded on the outer cell membrane

explanation: Steroid hormones easily pass through cell membranes, so their receptors are located inside the cell rather than on the surface. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which type of hormone is made of amino acid chains and dissolves easily in blood?
explanation: Peptide hormones are water-soluble proteins that travel freely in the bloodstream without needing carrier proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T3#GNS211_U1_T3_h2)

explanation: Precise dosing prevents overtreatment, which causes symptoms of hormone excess. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T8#GNS211_U1_T8_h6)

question: Which condition represents a life-threatening crisis of severe hypothyroidism?
explanation: Myxedema coma is the extreme, life-threatening manifestation of profound thyroid hormone deficiency. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T8#GNS211_U1_T8_h7)

question: What typically triggers an acute endocrine crisis in a patient with hyposecretion?

options.A: Consuming too much dietary sugar or sodium
options.B: Physical stress such as infection or trauma
options.C: Engaging in mild, routine physical exercise
options.D: Taking a single extra dose of replacement medication

explanation: Sudden stressors push a compromised endocrine system beyond its minimal reserve, precipitating acute crisis. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T8#GNS211_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is a key self-management instruction for patients taking lifelong hormone replacement?

options.A: Avoid all forms of physical activity
options.B: Double the dose whenever feeling energetic
options.C: Stop taking drugs once symptoms disappear

explanation: Consistent daily medication is essential because the body cannot produce its own hormones. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T8#GNS211_U1_T8_h8)

question: Why should a patient with chronic hyposecretion carry emergency medical identification?

options.A: To qualify for discounted prescription refills
options.B: To prove compliance with routine lab appointments
options.C: To ensure rapid treatment during an acute crisis
options.D: To exempt them from physical work restrictions

explanation: Medical ID alerts emergency responders to underlying hormone deficiencies if the patient becomes unresponsive. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T8#GNS211_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a hormone receptor on a target cell?

options.A: To transport hormones across the cell membrane
options.B: To break down excess hormones in the bloodstream
options.C: To bind a specific hormone and trigger cellular changes
options.D: To manufacture new hormones for systemic release

explanation: Receptors recognize and bind specific chemical messengers to initiate intracellular signaling pathways. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why do circulating hormones only affect specific target cells in the body?

options.A: Target cells express the matching receptors for those hormones
options.B: Target cells are located closer to the endocrine glands
options.C: Blood flow directs hormones exclusively to target organs
options.D: Non-target cells actively destroy circulating hormones

explanation: Cells without the specific receptor cannot bind the circulating hormone and therefore remain unaffected. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which of the following is classified as a lipid-soluble hormone?
explanation: Steroid hormones like cortisol are lipid-soluble and can easily cross cell membranes. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h2)

question: Where are the receptors for water-soluble hormones typically located?

options.A: On the outer surface of the cell membrane
options.C: Inside the fluid of the cell nucleus

explanation: Water-soluble hormones cannot cross the plasma membrane, so their binding sites must face the extracellular fluid. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h2)

question: What role does cyclic AMP (cAMP) play in water-soluble hormone signaling?

options.A: It acts as an intracellular second messenger
options.B: It serves as the primary hormone in the blood
options.C: It destroys the cell-surface receptor after use
options.D: It transports the hormone across the membrane

explanation: Second messengers like cAMP relay and amplify the hormonal signal inside the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the main advantage of using second messenger systems in cell signaling?

options.A: They allow the hormone to enter the cell nucleus directly
options.B: They prevent the breakdown of the original hormone molecule
options.C: They rapidly amplify the hormone's effect inside the cell
options.D: They eliminate the need for cell-surface receptors

explanation: A single hormone molecule binding to a surface receptor can activate many second messengers, producing a large physiological response. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h3)

question: What is the primary cellular action of a lipid-soluble hormone-receptor complex?

options.A: Altering gene transcription to synthesize new proteins
options.B: Blocking second messenger pathways in the cytoplasm
options.C: Activating membrane-bound enzymes like adenylate cyclase
options.D: Releasing calcium ions directly from the mitochondria

explanation: Lipid-soluble hormone complexes typically regulate gene expression in the nucleus to produce new proteins. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why is the physiological response to lipid-soluble hormones generally slower than water-soluble hormones?

options.A: They must wait for second messengers to build up in the blood
options.B: They travel much slower through the bloodstream to reach tissues
options.C: They require time to synthesize new proteins via gene transcription
options.D: They bind very weakly to their intracellular target receptors

explanation: Making new proteins through transcription and translation takes more time than activating existing enzymes. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h4)

question: What term describes a target cell increasing its receptor number due to low hormone levels?
explanation: Cells upregulate receptors to increase sensitivity when hormone concentrations are low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why does prolonged high exposure to a hormone lead to receptor downregulation?

options.A: To convert the water-soluble hormone into a lipid-soluble one
options.B: To speed up the clearance of hormones from the bloodstream
options.C: To protect the cell from excessive and harmful overstimulation
options.D: To force the endocrine gland to stop hormone production

explanation: Downregulation reduces cellular responsiveness, preventing damage from chronic hormone excess. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h5)

question: What is the primary defect in peripheral tissues during early type 2 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Destruction of the pancreas by antibodies

explanation: Type 2 diabetes typically features normal or high insulin levels, but target cells fail to respond due to receptor resistance. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h6)

question: What happens to hormone blood levels when a genetic mutation causes complete receptor insensitivity?

options.A: Hormone levels drop to zero because they are destroyed
options.B: Hormone levels decrease due to immediate negative feedback
options.C: Hormone levels often rise as the body tries to compensate
options.D: Hormone levels remain completely unaffected and stable

explanation: When receptors fail, the lack of tissue response removes negative feedback, prompting glands to secrete more hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T9#GNS211_U1_T9_h6)

question: What percentage of total adult body weight does the skin represent?
explanation: The skin is the largest organ and accounts for approximately 16 percent of total adult body weight. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why must nurses evaluate skin condition during routine physical assessments?

options.A: Epidermal cells regulate blood pressure directly
options.B: The skin produces all vital body hormones daily
options.C: Subcutaneous fat controls core body temperature
options.D: Skin changes often reflect internal systemic diseases

explanation: Skin manifestations frequently signal underlying pathological processes occurring inside the body. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which epidermal layer contains actively dividing cells responsible for continuous skin renewal?
explanation: The stratum basale rests on the basement membrane and contains stem cells that constantly divide to produce new skin cells. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h2)

question: Where is the stratum lucidum typically located on the human body?
explanation: The stratum lucidum is an extra protective layer found only in areas of thick skin, such as the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which skin layer contains the blood vessels and sensory receptors?
explanation: The dermis is richly vascularized and packed with nerve endings and receptors, unlike the avascular epidermis. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the primary function of dermal papillae in the papillary layer?

options.A: Storing excess subcutaneous fat for energy
options.B: Forming fingerprints and anchoring layers together
options.C: Producing large amounts of protective melanin
options.D: Secreting sweat to cool down the body

explanation: Dermal papillae create uneven projections that firmly anchor the epidermis to the dermis and form unique friction ridges like fingerprints. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h3)

question: What type of tissue is predominantly found within the hypodermis?
explanation: The hypodermis contains a large amount of adipose or fat tissue, which provides insulation and energy storage. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h4)

question: A key role of the subcutaneous layer in overall health is...

options.B: Generating new cells for the epidermis
options.C: Secreting oils to lubricate hair shafts
options.D: Insulating the body against heat loss

explanation: The layer of fat in the hypodermis traps body heat, serving as vital thermal insulation against cold environments. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h4)

question: What substance do sebaceous glands secrete to keep skin waterproof and soft?
explanation: Sebaceous glands produce sebum, an oily secretion that lubricates the skin and hair shafts. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which of the following structures is considered an epidermal appendage?
explanation: Nails, hair, and sweat glands are all specialized epidermal derivatives known as skin appendages. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h5)

question: Which vitamin is synthesized in the skin through exposure to sunlight?
explanation: Sunlight exposure triggers the skin to convert a cholesterol precursor into active vitamin D for bone metabolism. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is vitamin D synthesis by the skin important for the human body?

options.A: It prevents the development of skin cancer
options.B: It is required for normal calcium absorption
options.C: It maintains the normal color of epidermis
options.D: It stimulates sweat gland production rates

explanation: Vitamin D produced by the skin enables the intestines to absorb dietary calcium, supporting strong bones. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which specialized cell produces the pigment responsible for skin color?
explanation: Melanocytes located in the basal layer produce melanin, which determines skin pigmentation and protects against UV radiation. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h7)

question: How does the skin respond when the core body temperature becomes too high?

options.B: Blood vessels constrict to trap internal heat
options.D: Dermal blood vessels dilate to release heat

explanation: Vasodilation of dermal blood vessels brings warm blood closer to the body surface so excess heat can radiate into the air. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T1#GNS211_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary physical function of the integumentary system?

options.A: Synthesizing all essential human vitamins independently
options.B: Pumping oxygenated blood throughout deep tissue layers
options.C: Providing a protective barrier against external hazards
options.D: Producing white blood cells for the immune response

explanation: The integumentary system primarily acts as a shield protecting internal body structures from pathogens, chemicals, and physical injury. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is skin assessment particularly valuable during a general nursing physical examination?

options.A: It provides a definitive measurement of internal core body temperature
options.B: It directly measures the exact rate of cellular metabolism
options.C: It accurately determines the total white blood cell count
options.D: It gives immediate clues about hydration and systemic health

explanation: Changes in skin color, turgor, and moisture reflect underlying fluid balance, circulation, and overall medical conditions. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which epidermal layer contains actively dividing stem cells?
explanation: The stratum basale rests on the basement membrane and houses the mitotic stem cells that continuously supply new cells to upper layers. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h2)

question: Where is the stratum lucidum typically located on the human body?

options.C: Palms and soles of the feet

explanation: This clear layer of dead keratinocytes is exclusively found in areas subjected to heavy friction, such as thick skin on palms and soles. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h2)

question: What type of tissue primarily makes up the reticular layer of the dermis?
explanation: The reticular layer consists of thick bundles of collagen and elastin fibers arranged in a dense irregular network that provides strength in multiple directions. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary function of dermal papillae in the papillary layer?

options.A: Storing excess fat for long-term energy reserves
options.B: Producing melanin pigment to protect against UV rays
options.C: Secreting oily sebum to lubricate skin surfaces
options.D: Forming unique fingerprints and housing touch receptors

explanation: Dermal papillae create interlocking ridges with the epidermis, forming fingerprint patterns and bringing blood vessels and nerve endings close to the surface. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h3)

question: What primary tissue type dominates the hypodermis layer?
explanation: The hypodermis contains a large amount of fat-storing adipose cells that provide insulation, padding, and energy storage. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why is the hypodermis chosen as the anatomical site for subcutaneous insulin injections?

options.A: It lacks any nerve fibers, preventing pain during needle insertion
options.B: It has a loose structure with slow, steady absorption rates
options.C: It contains massive blood vessels for instant systemic distribution
options.D: It actively neutralizes injected medications before they work

explanation: The loose connective and fatty nature of the hypodermis allows injected medications to be absorbed gradually into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h4)

question: Which gland type is primarily responsible for cooling the body through watery sweat production?
explanation: Eccrine glands are distributed all over the skin surface and secrete a watery fluid that cools the body down when body temperature rises. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary function of sebum produced by sebaceous glands?

options.A: Producing vitamin D precursors using sunlight exposure
options.B: Anchoring hair shafts securely into the dermal layer
options.C: Lubricating and waterproofing the skin and hair
options.D: Regulating core body temperature during heavy fevers

explanation: Sebum is an oily substance that prevents skin and hair from drying out while also providing mild antibacterial properties. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h5)

question: Which skin receptors are primarily responsible for detecting deep pressure and vibration?
explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors located deep in the dermis that sense deep pressure and high-frequency vibration. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h6)

question: What physiological action does the skin take when core body temperature drops significantly?

options.A: Dermal blood vessels dilate to release excess heat
options.B: Sebaceous glands secrete more oily sebum onto the surface
options.C: Dermal blood vessels constrict to conserve core heat
options.D: Eccrine sweat glands increase production of watery sweat

explanation: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin surface, minimizing heat loss from the blood to the external environment. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T2#GNS211_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the outermost layer of the epidermis called?
explanation: The stratum corneum consists of dead, keratinized cells that form the tough outer protective shell of the skin. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h1)

question: What is the main job of desmosomes in the epidermis?

options.A: They secrete sweat to keep the skin acidic.
options.B: They produce melanin pigments to absorb UV radiation.
options.C: They produce lipids that block water-soluble toxins.
options.D: They bind skin cells firmly together so they don't tear apart.

explanation: Desmosomes act as strong cellular anchors that prevent epidermal cells from pulling apart under mechanical stress. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which protein in the dermis gives the skin its strength and prevents tearing?
explanation: Collagen fibers form a dense network in the dermis that gives the skin structural strength against pulling forces. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient falls and hits their thigh. Which skin layer mainly absorbs this blunt shock?
explanation: The hypodermis contains fat tissue which acts as a cushioning pad against blunt physical trauma. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the typical pH range of the skin's protective acid mantle?
explanation: The skin surface is naturally acidic, with a pH ranging between 4.5 and 5.5 to discourage bacterial growth. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why is the oily skin secretion called sebum important for chemical defense?

options.A: It stimulates antibody production by local immune cells.
options.B: It neutralizes alkaline toxins that enter the skin.
options.C: It keeps the skin hydrated by trapping water molecules.
options.D: It contains fatty acids that stop harmful bacteria from growing.

explanation: Sebum contributes to the acidic barrier and has natural antimicrobial properties that restrict harmful bacteria. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which specialized immune cells live in the epidermis to spot foreign invaders?
explanation: Langerhans cells act as immune sentinels within the epidermis, capturing foreign particles and triggering immune responses. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h4)

question: What do Langerhans cells do after they capture a germ in the skin?

options.A: They travel to lymph nodes to present the germ to T-cells.
options.B: They release oil to chemically neutralize the germ.
options.C: They transform into skin cells to repair damaged tissue.
options.D: They produce collagen to wall off the infected area.

explanation: After capturing foreign particles, Langerhans cells travel through the lymph system to activate the body's broader immune response. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h4)

question: Where are melanocytes mainly found in the epidermis?
explanation: Melanocytes live in the deepest layer of the epidermis, the stratum basale, close to dividing cells they protect. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h5)

question: How does melanin protect skin cells from ultraviolet radiation?

options.A: It neutralizes free radicals caused by burns.
options.B: It forms a protective cap over the cell nucleus to absorb UV rays.
options.C: It thickens the outer skin layer to block light.
options.D: It increases blood flow to cool down sunburnt tissue.

explanation: Melanin granules position themselves over the DNA inside cell nuclei to shield it from sun damage. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h5)

question: Which skin structure stops body water from evaporating into the air?
explanation: The oil-rich matrix between cells in the stratum corneum creates a waterproof barrier that prevents dehydration. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h6)

question: How does the skin respond when your core body temperature gets too high?

options.A: Blood vessels in the dermis constrict to trap heat inside.
options.B: Blood vessels in the dermis widen and sweat production increases.
options.C: Oil glands produce more sebum to block heat.
options.D: The fat layer thickens to insulate the body.

explanation: Widening blood vessels brings warm blood to the surface while sweat evaporation cools the body down. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h6)

question: A patient with severe second-degree burns is at immediate risk for which main problem?

options.A: Thickening of the outer skin layer
options.B: Severe fluid loss and electrolyte imbalance
options.C: Dark skin patches from too much melanin

explanation: Destroying the outer skin barrier removes the body's protection against massive water and salt loss. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the most important nursing action when caring for a patient with damaged skin?

options.A: Keeping the patient completely still to protect fat layers
options.B: Using strict sterile technique for all wound and dressing care
options.C: Applying harsh alkaline soaps to the skin
options.D: Encouraging long exposure to sunlight to boost melanin

explanation: A broken skin barrier leaves the patient wide open to infection, making strict cleanliness and sterile care essential. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which body part is mainly responsible for exchanging heat with the outside environment?
explanation: The skin acts as the main boundary between the body and the outside environment, helping to balance body heat. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why is keeping the body temperature around 37°C so important?

options.A: It prevents all forms of physical fatigue
options.B: It protects vital organs from extreme temperatures
options.C: It increases red blood cell destruction
options.D: It stops the production of waste products

explanation: A stable core temperature ensures cells work properly and protects internal organs from damage caused by extreme heat or cold. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h1)

question: Which skin gland produces a watery fluid that cools the body when it evaporates?
explanation: Eccrine sweat glands release watery fluid onto the skin surface, which absorbs body heat and cools you down as it evaporates. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the main job of the fat layer under the skin (subcutaneous fat) when you are exposed to cold?

options.A: Opening blood vessels to let out trapped heat
options.B: Producing sweat to cool the skin
options.C: Providing insulation to keep heat from escaping the body

explanation: Subcutaneous fat acts as an insulating layer that slows down how fast body heat escapes into the cold air. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the body's main thermostat?
explanation: The hypothalamus contains the control center that monitors temperature changes and tells the body how to respond. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h3)

question: Where does the hypothalamus get temperature information from?

options.A: The outer layer of the epidermis only
options.B: Receptors in the skin and inside the core
options.C: Skeletal muscles and bone marrow only

explanation: To keep body temperature balanced, the hypothalamus continuously receives signals from both surface skin receptors and internal core organs. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h3)

question: What happens to blood vessels in the skin when the body needs to lose extra heat?
explanation: Vasodilation widens surface blood vessels, bringing warm blood closer to the skin so the heat can escape into the air. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h4)

question: How does sweat on the skin help cool the body down?

options.A: Fluid secretion directly lowers blood temperature
options.B: Sweat creates an insulating layer against warmth
options.C: Heat is drawn away from the body as the moisture evaporates
options.D: Moisture reacts with fat to make cold energy

explanation: As sweat changes from liquid to vapor, it absorbs and removes thermal energy from the skin surface. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h4)

question: What is the term for rapid, involuntary muscle contractions that generate heat when you are cold?
explanation: Shivering makes skeletal muscles work quickly, turning chemical energy into body heat. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h5)

question: Why does narrowing of skin blood vessels (vasoconstriction) help you survive in the cold?

options.B: It keeps warm blood deep inside the core away from the cold skin
options.C: It rushes blood to fingers and toes to stop freezing

explanation: By narrowing surface blood vessels, the body keeps warm blood near vital internal organs and reduces heat loss. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the medical term for a core body temperature that drops dangerously below 35°C?
explanation: Hypothermia happens when the core body temperature falls below normal operating limits, which is generally under 35°C. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h6)

question: What primary environmental factor contributes to the development of heat stroke in high temperatures?

options.A: Excessive shivering caused by sudden drafts
options.B: Sudden vasodilation of deep core blood vessels
options.C: Rapid increase in subcutaneous adipose tissue insulation
options.D: High humidity that prevents effective sweat evaporation

explanation: High ambient humidity stops sweat from evaporating off the skin, trapping heat inside the body and causing core temperatures to rise rapidly. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T4#GNS211_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is the outermost layer of the skin called?
explanation: The epidermis is the outermost, avascular layer of the skin that forms the primary barrier against the external environment. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h1)

question: Where are blood vessels and nerve endings primarily located within the skin structure?
explanation: The dermis is the vascularized middle layer that houses blood vessels, nerve endings, and accessory structures like sweat glands. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which specialized cells in the epidermis play a key role in immune defense?
explanation: Langerhans cells are resident dendritic cells in the epidermis that capture antigens and initiate immune responses. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h2)

question: What primary skin property stops harmful bacteria from growing on the surface?
explanation: The skin maintains a slightly acidic surface, which creates an environment that prevents harmful bacteria from multiplying. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h2)

question: What happens to blood vessels in the skin when body temperature goes up?
explanation: Vasodilation means blood vessels widen, bringing warm blood closer to the skin surface so excess body heat can escape. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient with a high fever has warm, flushed skin. What is the body doing?
explanation: Warm and flushed skin during a fever shows that surface blood vessels have widened to help release extra body heat. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h3)

question: Which skin receptors are primarily responsible for detecting deep pressure and vibration?
explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are deep dermal receptors specialized for detecting heavy pressure and rapid vibrations. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h4)

question: What type of feelings are detected by free nerve endings in the skin?
explanation: Free nerve endings reach into the skin layers to pick up sensations like pain, heat, and cold. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h4)

question: Which vitamin is made in the skin when exposed to sunlight?
explanation: Sunlight exposure on the skin triggers the production of Vitamin D, which the body needs for various functions. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the main job of the active form of Vitamin D produced by the skin?
explanation: Active Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium from food, which is essential for strong bones and teeth. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h5)

question: What waste products are removed from the body through sweat?
explanation: Sweat is mostly water, but it also carries away dissolved salts and small amounts of urea waste. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary function of sebum produced by sebaceous glands?
explanation: Sebum coats the skin and hair shaft to prevent excessive moisture loss and maintain a pliable barrier. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h6)

question: How does the skin act as a blood reservoir during heavy exercise?

options.A: The outer skin layer stretches to hold extra blood
options.B: Fat tissue releases stored red blood cells
options.C: Blood vessels in the skin constrict to send blood to muscles
options.D: Sweat glands turn fluid into circulating blood

explanation: When you exercise hard, skin blood vessels narrow to redirect blood flow toward the working muscles. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h7)

question: What property allows certain patches or creams to pass through the outer skin layer?
explanation: Substances that dissolve well in fats can easily cross the lipid-rich outer layer of the skin. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h7)

question: Why is a bedridden patient at high risk for pressure sores?

options.A: They cannot feel discomfort to make them shift positions
options.B: Immune cells in their skin destroy collagen
options.C: Their skin blood vessels stay permanently widened
options.D: Their sweat glands stop making protective oils

explanation: If a patient cannot feel discomfort or move easily, they stay in one position too long, cutting off blood flow and damaging tissues. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which physical sign points directly to reduced blood flow and changes in body temperature?
explanation: Cool and pale skin usually happens when blood vessels narrow, reducing blood flow to the surface. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T5#GNS211_U2_T5_h8)

question: Which primary germ layer forms the entire nervous system?
explanation: The nervous system develops directly from the embryonic ectoderm layer during early development. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the first visible sign of nervous system development in the embryo?

options.A: Complete closure of the anterior neuropore
options.B: Migration of neural crest cells into the trunk
options.C: Thickening of the ectoderm into a neural plate

explanation: The neural plate forms when signals cause the embryonic ectoderm to thicken, marking the start of nervous system development. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the hollow structure that forms the early central nervous system during embryogenesis?
explanation: The neural plate rolls and fuses to create the neural tube, which eventually forms the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h2)

question: A newborn has an open spinal defect because the lower end of the neural tube failed to close. What is this developmental process called?
explanation: The failure of the neuropores to close properly happens during the neurulation stage of embryonic development. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the primary forebrain vesicle?
explanation: The prosencephalon is the primary forebrain vesicle that later divides into the telencephalon and diencephalon. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which layer of the developing neural tube eventually forms the white matter of the central nervous system?
explanation: The marginal zone is the outermost layer of the neural tube where nerve fibers bundle together to form white matter. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which part of the developing spinal cord handles motor functions?
explanation: The basal plate is located on the lower side of the neural tube and gives rise to motor neurons. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which embryonic cells give rise to peripheral nervous system structures like sensory ganglia and Schwann cells?
explanation: Neural crest cells break away during neural tube closure and migrate to form much of the peripheral nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h4)

question: What are the specialized glial cells that guide migrating neurons during brain development called?
explanation: Radial glial cells act as physical pathways along which young neurons crawl to reach their correct locations in the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h5)

question: How do growing nerve fibers find their correct target cells over long distances in the embryo?

options.A: Using chemical guidance cues at their growing tips
options.C: Relying entirely on blood flow through capillaries
options.D: Following random electrical impulses from the heart

explanation: Growth cones at the tips of developing nerve fibers read chemical attraction and repulsion signals in the environment to steer correctly. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which glial cell type produces myelin in the central nervous system?
explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate axons inside the brain and spinal cord, while Schwann cells do this in the peripheral nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of myelination along developing nerve fibers?

options.A: To anchor neurons permanently in tissue layers
options.B: To increase the speed of electrical impulse conduction
options.C: To provide nutrition and blood supply to neurons
options.D: To prevent the formation of unwanted synapses

explanation: Myelin acts as an insulation layer that allows nerve impulses to travel much faster down the axon. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which maternal supplement helps prevent neural tube defects when taken early in pregnancy?
explanation: Folic acid is essential for proper neural tube closure and significantly lowers the risk of conditions like spina bifida. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h7)

question: A baby is born with an opening at the lower back that exposes the spinal membranes due to incomplete neural tube closure. What is this condition called?
explanation: Spina bifida is a neural tube defect caused by the failure of the lower end of the neural tube to close properly during early development. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T1#GNS211_U3_T1_h7)

question: What primary function do the cerebral cortex motor regions control?
explanation: The motor regions within the cerebral cortex are primarily dedicated to generating and controlling voluntary skeletal muscle movements. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h1)

question: Why does the cerebral cortex feature folds like gyri and sulci?

options.A: To maximize surface area within the skull
options.B: To protect the brain from blunt trauma injuries
options.C: To separate sensory and motor blood supplies
options.D: To increase the speed of cranial nerve impulses

explanation: Folding creates a larger cortical surface area inside the limited space of the cranial vault to house more neurons. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h1)

question: Brodmann area 4 corresponds to which specific brain region?
explanation: Brodmann area 4 is anatomically located in the precentral gyrus and is identified as the primary motor cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h2)

question: A lesion in the left primary motor cortex will result in weakness on which side of the body?
explanation: Motor pathways cross over to the opposite side of the body, meaning the left hemisphere controls the right limbs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h2)

question: What determines the amount of cortical space a body part occupies on the motor homunculus?

options.A: The distance of the muscle from the spinal cord
options.B: The degree of fine motor control needed
options.C: The physical mass and weight of the body part
options.D: The total number of bone joints in the region

explanation: Body parts capable of intricate, precise movements, like the fingers and lips, receive a larger area on the homunculus. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h3)

question: Why do the hands and fingers occupy a much larger cortical area than the thigh?

options.A: Thigh movements are controlled entirely by the cerebellum
options.B: Hands require more intricate and precise muscle control
options.C: The hands are located closer to the frontal lobe
options.D: Thigh muscles contain fewer sensory nerve endings

explanation: Cortical representation is proportional to motor precision, giving hands vastly more territory than large postural muscles like thighs. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h3)

question: What is the primary function of the supplementary motor area?

options.A: Processing raw visual signals from the retina
options.B: Interpreting spoken words and auditory tones
options.C: Regulating core body temperature and thirst
options.D: Programming internal sequences of complex movements

explanation: The supplementary motor area plans and coordinates complex movement sequences that originate internally rather than from immediate reflexes. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h4)

question: Which motor region typically responds directly to external visual cues to guide limb posture?
explanation: The premotor cortex specializes in preparing and guiding movements based on external sensory information like sight or sound. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h4)

question: In which cerebral lobe is Broca's area typically located?
explanation: Broca's area is situated in the inferior frontal gyrus of the frontal lobe, close to the motor strip for facial muscles. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h5)

question: A patient with damage to Broca's area will most likely exhibit which symptom?

options.A: Difficulty speaking fluently despite understanding language
options.B: Complete inability to hear or process spoken words
options.C: Loss of spatial awareness on the left side
options.D: Total paralysis of both lower limbs and feet

explanation: Expressive aphasia impairs speech production and articulation while leaving language comprehension relatively well preserved. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h5)

question: Which pathway is primarily responsible for fast, skilled voluntary movements of the hands?
explanation: The pyramidal tracts, especially the corticospinal tract, deliver direct commands for rapid, fine voluntary motor actions. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h6)

question: What clinical feature is most characteristic of damage to the extrapyramidal motor system?

options.A: Complete flaccid paralysis of all four limbs
options.B: Total loss of cutaneous sensation to touch
options.C: Involuntary movements and abnormal muscle tone
options.D: Inability to perceive light and visual shapes

explanation: The extrapyramidal system controls posture and tone, so its lesion manifests as tremors, rigidity, or unwanted movements. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h6)

question: What physical sign is commonly associated with an upper motor neuron lesion?
explanation: Upper motor neuron damage removes inhibitory control from the brain, resulting in exaggerated reflexes and spasticity. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h7)

question: Which clinical finding helps distinguish a lower motor neuron lesion from an upper motor neuron lesion?

options.A: Presence of a positive Babinski reflex response
options.C: Spastic increase in resting limb muscle tone
options.D: Marked muscle wasting and flaccid paralysis

explanation: Lower motor neuron lesions cut the direct neural link to muscles, causing flaccidity, absent reflexes, and rapid muscle atrophy. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T10#GNS211_U3_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary function of sensory areas in the cerebral cortex?

options.B: Translate environmental stimuli into conscious perception
options.C: Regulate autonomic heart rate and respiration
options.D: Generate abstract reasoning and emotional responses

explanation: Sensory areas receive signals from the peripheral nerves and process them so the brain can consciously perceive them. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h1)

question: A lesion in a motor area of the cerebral cortex will most directly affect which bodily function?
explanation: Motor areas are specifically responsible for planning and executing voluntary skeletal muscle movements. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h1)

question: In which lobe of the brain is the primary somatosensory cortex found?
explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex sits specifically within the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h2)

question: Why do the lips and fingertips have large representations on the sensory homunculus?

options.A: They are physically the largest body parts
options.B: They have many sensory receptors for fine touch
options.C: They require constant voluntary motor control
options.D: They are located closest to the cerebral cortex

explanation: Areas of the body with dense sensory receptors and fine tactile discrimination require more cortical processing space. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h2)

question: Where is the primary visual cortex located?
explanation: The primary visual cortex is situated at the very back of the brain within the occipital lobe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h3)

question: A patient can see an object but cannot name it due to brain damage. Which area is likely affected?
explanation: Visual association areas interpret raw visual data from the primary cortex to give meaning to what is seen. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h3)

question: Which lobe of the brain houses the primary auditory cortex?
explanation: The primary auditory cortex is located within the superior temporal gyrus of the temporal lobe. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the main job of the auditory association area compared to the primary auditory cortex?

options.A: Generating motor responses to loud noises
options.B: Balancing fluid pressures within the inner ear
options.C: Receiving initial electrical impulses from the cochlea
options.D: Interpreting the meaning of sounds like speech or music

explanation: While the primary cortex registers basic sound qualities, the association area analyzes and gives meaning to those sounds. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h4)

question: Where is the primary gustatory cortex located?
explanation: Taste perception is processed primarily within the insula and the lower parietal operculum. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h5)

question: Why do certain odors often trigger strong emotional memories?

options.A: Olfactory neurons are the only cells that directly touch the skin
options.B: The olfactory cortex connects closely with the limbic system
options.C: Smell signals bypass the thalamus entirely to reach the frontal lobe
options.D: The gustatory cortex works together with smell receptors

explanation: The anatomical proximity between the olfactory cortex and limbic structures ties smell directly to emotion and memory. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h5)

question: Which cranial nerve transmits balance and equilibrium signals from the inner ear to the brain?
explanation: Cranial nerve VIII carries both auditory and vestibular information from the inner ear to the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h6)

question: How does the vestibular cortex differ in organization from most other sensory cortices?

options.A: It processes sensory data without input from peripheral receptors
options.B: It sends signals directly to muscles without the cerebral cortex
options.C: It is spread across multiple regions in the parietal and temporal lobes
options.D: It is located entirely within the occipital lobe

explanation: The vestibular cortex lacks a single dedicated gyrus and is instead spread across the parieto-insular network. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h6)

question: What is the term for recognizing an object by touch without using visual cues?
explanation: Stereognosis relies on sensory association areas to integrate tactile and spatial information for object recognition. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary role of sensory association areas in the cerebral cortex?

options.B: Synthesize raw inputs into meaningful, unified perceptions
options.C: Regulate basic metabolic processes within brain tissue
options.D: Receive initial electrical impulses directly from sensory organs

explanation: Association areas take basic sensory data from primary cortices and combine them to form complex, recognizable perceptions. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h7)

question: A stroke affecting the right primary somatosensory cortex will most likely impair touch sensation on which part of the body?

options.D: Both upper and lower extremities equally

explanation: Sensory pathways cross over, meaning damage to one side of the cerebral cortex affects the contralateral side of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h8)

question: Which nursing finding is expected when assessing a patient with a lesion in the primary visual cortex?

options.A: Inability to speak clearly despite moving the tongue
options.B: Visual field defects or cortical blindness
options.C: Loss of balance and severe inner ear vertigo
options.D: Complete inability to feel hot or cold temperatures

explanation: The primary visual cortex processes incoming sight data, so injury directly results in visual impairments like field cuts. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T11#GNS211_U3_T11_h8)

question: Which brain structure pairs with the caudate nucleus to form the striatum?
explanation: The putamen and the caudate nucleus together make up the striatum, which serves as the primary receiving area for the basal ganglia. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h1)

question: What is the main role of the substantia nigra in the basal ganglia circuit?

options.A: Providing sensory relay to the cerebral cortex
options.B: Initiating primary sensory signals from the periphery
options.C: Delivering dopamine via the nigrostriatal pathway
options.D: Storing cerebrospinal fluid for ventricular pressure

explanation: Dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra send critical chemical signals to the striatum to modulate motor activity. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h1)

question: What is the net effect of the direct pathway on motor activity?
explanation: The direct pathway reduces output from the basal ganglia, releasing the thalamus from inhibition so movement can proceed. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h2)

question: In the indirect pathway, which structure directly stimulates the internal globus pallidus?
explanation: The subthalamic nucleus sends excitatory glutamatergic projections to the internal segment of the globus pallidus during indirect pathway activation. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h2)

question: Besides movement, what non-motor function involves the basal ganglia?
explanation: Circuits passing through the ventral striatum link basal ganglia function to reward processing, motivation, and procedural learning. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h3)

question: How do the basal ganglia help coordinate voluntary movement?

options.A: By providing direct sensory feedback from active muscle spindles
options.B: By selecting desired movement plans and suppressing unwanted ones
options.C: By generating initial electrical impulses within spinal motor neurons
options.D: By directly transmitting motor commands down the corticospinal tract

explanation: The basal ganglia act as a gatekeeper, promoting chosen motor programs while holding competing movements in check. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h3)

question: Loss of cells in which brain area directly causes Parkinson's disease?
explanation: Parkinson's disease results from the loss of dopamine-producing cells in the pars compacta of the substantia nigra. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h4)

question: Why does Huntington's disease cause continuous, uncontrolled movements?

options.A: Hyperactivity of the subthalamic nucleus eliminates all thalamic suppression
options.B: Excessive dopamine production floods the motor cortex with uninhibited signals
options.C: Degeneration of neurons in the indirect pathway reduces inhibitory control over movement
options.D: Destruction of the direct pathway forces erratic muscle contractions

explanation: The loss of striatal neurons in the indirect pathway removes the normal braking mechanism, leading to hyperkinetic movements like chorea. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h4)

question: A patient with Parkinson's disease has a shuffling gait and leans forward. What is the priority nursing intervention?

options.A: Perform a formal visual acuity examination
options.B: Restrict all physical movement to prevent fatigue

explanation: Postural instability and festinating gait greatly increase the risk of falls, making safety and fall precautions an immediate priority. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h5)

question: Which finding is most characteristic of basal ganglia motor dysfunction during physical assessment?

options.A: Flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes
options.C: Loss of conscious sensation in the lower limbs

explanation: Basal ganglia disorders classically present with extrapyramidal signs, including resting tremors, rigidity, and altered movement speeds. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T12#GNS211_U3_T12_h5)

question: What is the primary nickname often given to the limbic system in neurology?
