explanation: The lens changes shape to adjust focus for near and distant objects after the cornea does the initial light bending. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h1)

question: What happens to the pupil when you walk from a dark room into bright sunlight?

options.A: It gets bigger to catch more light
options.B: It pushes forward to help focus
options.C: It flattens to reduce light bending
options.D: It gets smaller to let less light in

explanation: The pupil constricts in bright light to protect the sensitive cells inside the retina from being overloaded. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h2)

question: What happens inside the eye when you look at something very close to you?

options.A: Supporting fibers pull the lens flat
options.B: The iris opens up wide to let in more light
options.C: Ciliary muscles relax and the lens flattens
options.D: Ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens

explanation: When the ciliary muscle tightens, the supporting fibers loosen, allowing the natural elasticity of the lens to make it rounder for near vision. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h2)

question: Which cells in the retina are mainly responsible for helping us see at night and in dim light?
explanation: Rods contain high amounts of a pigment called rhodopsin, making them very sensitive to low levels of light. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h3)

question: What happens inside a rod cell when light hits it?

options.A: Sodium channels open and the cell fires an electric impulse
options.B: Potassium rushes in to reset the resting state
options.C: Sodium channels close and the cell becomes more negative inside
options.D: Chemical release increases to stimulate nearby cells

explanation: When light hits the rod cell, it causes sodium channels to close, leading to a drop in the release of chemical messengers. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which cranial nerve carries visual messages from the retina to the brain?
explanation: The optic nerve, or cranial nerve II, is formed by nerve fibers carrying visual signals away from the eyeball. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h4)

question: What happens to visual nerve fibers as they meet at the optic chiasm?

options.A: Fibers from the outer side of the retina cross over while inner fibers stay straight
options.B: Only the fibers from the left eye cross over to the right side
options.C: Nerve fibers from the inner side of each retina cross over to the opposite side of the brain
options.D: All visual signals stop and mix together before heading to the brain

explanation: This crossing over at the optic chiasm blends signals from both eyes, which is essential for depth perception. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h4)

question: Why does it take time for your eyes to adjust when you walk into a very dark room?

options.A: The visual center in the brain needs a long rest
options.B: It takes time for the light-sensitive pigment in rod cells to rebuild
options.C: All the cone cells get tired out at the same time
options.D: The pupil takes a long time to open up

explanation: Dark adaptation relies on the chemical process of rebuilding rhodopsin stores after bright light has used them up. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h5)

question: How is the human eye able to see and distinguish many different colors?

options.A: By constantly changing the fluid inside the eye
options.B: By switching back and forth between rods and cones during the day
options.C: By filtering light through different shapes of the cornea
options.D: By comparing the combined signals from three different types of cone cells

explanation: Color vision depends on red, green, and blue cones working together so the brain can interpret different shades. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T6#GNS211_U4_T6_h5)

question: What physical property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
explanation: Frequency measures the speed of wave cycles, which directly corresponds to the perceived pitch of a sound. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h1)

question: How does the ear function as a biological transducer?

options.A: It converts mechanical sound energy into electrical nerve impulses
options.B: It changes air pressure directly into cerebrospinal fluid waves
options.C: It amplifies high-frequency waves into thermal energy
options.D: It filters out background noise using chemical buffers

explanation: Transduction involves changing one form of energy into another, which the ear accomplishes by turning physical sound waves into neural signals. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h1)

question: Which structure connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx?
explanation: The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure between the middle ear and the atmosphere by connecting to the nasopharynx. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h2)

question: What are the three bones of the middle ear called collectively?
explanation: The malleus, incus, and stapes are known as the auditory ossicles. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h2)

question: Why does the middle ear act as an impedance-matching transformer?

options.A: To convert high-frequency sounds into low-frequency vibrations
options.B: To prevent energy loss when sound moves from air to fluid
options.C: To equalize the blood pressure inside the temporal bone
options.D: To cool down the inner ear fluids during high-intensity noise

explanation: Fluid offers more resistance to sound waves than air does, requiring mechanical amplification by the ossicles to transfer energy efficiently. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h3)

question: Which bone of the middle ear directly contacts the oval window?
explanation: The footplate of the stapes fits directly into the oval window to transmit vibrations into the inner ear. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h3)

question: Where do pressure waves in the cochlea ultimately dissipate?
explanation: The round window acts as a pressure relief valve for the fluid-filled chambers of the cochlea. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h4)

question: How are different sound frequencies mapped along the basilar membrane?

options.A: Frequencies are sorted by amplitude rather than location on the membrane
options.B: All frequencies stimulate the entire membrane with equal intensity
options.C: High frequencies peak near the base, low frequencies peak near the apex
options.D: High frequencies peak near the apex, low frequencies peak near the base

explanation: The stiffness and width gradient of the basilar membrane causes high pitches to register at the stiff base and low pitches at the flexible apex. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h4)

question: What is the name of the sensory receptors responsible for hearing?
explanation: Hair cells within the Organ of Corti contain stereocilia that transduce mechanical movement into electrical signals. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h5)

question: What triggers the opening of ion channels in the stereocilia during hearing?

options.A: Electrical discharge from nearby bone cells
options.B: Chemical binding of hormones in the fluid
options.C: Mechanical bending caused by motion against the tectorial membrane
options.D: Thermal expansion of fluid during loud noise

explanation: The movement of the basilar membrane creates a shearing force that physically bends the stereocilia, opening mechanically gated ion channels. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h5)

question: Which cranial nerve transmits auditory impulses from the inner ear to the brain?
explanation: The vestibulocochlear nerve carries both hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the central nervous system. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the superior olivary complex in the auditory pathway?

options.A: Storing long-term memory of spoken words
options.B: Converting electrical signals back into mechanical fluid waves
options.C: Filtering out background noise before it reaches the thalamus
options.D: Localizing sound by comparing timing and intensity from both ears

explanation: The superior olivary complex is the first place in the brain where auditory information from both ears converges to help determine sound direction. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h6)

question: In which lobe of the brain is the primary auditory cortex located?
explanation: The temporal lobe houses the auditory cortex, which handles conscious perception and interpretation of sounds. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h7)

question: What does tonotopic organization in the auditory cortex mean?

options.A: Loud sounds are processed in the left hemisphere and soft sounds in the right
options.B: All sound volumes are processed equally across the cortex
options.C: Musical tones are stored separately from spoken language
options.D: Specific cortical neurons respond preferentially to specific sound frequencies

explanation: Tonotopy preserves the frequency map of the cochlea all the way through to the primary auditory cortex. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T7#GNS211_U4_T7_h7)

question: What type of equilibrium detects head position when the body is stationary?
explanation: Static equilibrium is responsible for monitoring and maintaining the position of the head when the body is not moving. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h1)

question: Why is dynamic equilibrium important during physical movement?

options.A: It helps detect rapid head rotation and acceleration.
options.B: It regulates body temperature in hot weather.
options.C: It maintains steady heart rates while running.
options.D: It controls blood pressure during sudden standing.

explanation: Dynamic equilibrium monitors changes in motion, specifically rotation and acceleration, to keep the body stable while moving. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h1)

question: Where is the vestibular apparatus located in the human body?

options.A: Inside the temporal bone of the inner ear
options.B: At the base of the brainstem near the cerebellum
options.C: Within the middle ear cavity behind the eardrum
options.D: Inside the outer ear canal near the pinna

explanation: The entire vestibular apparatus is housed safely within the temporal bone of the inner ear. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h2)

question: What is the name of the fluid found inside the membranous labyrinth?
explanation: Endolymph fills the interior of the membranous labyrinth and plays a direct role in stimulating vestibular hair cells. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h2)

question: What is the name of the enlarged base of each semicircular canal?
explanation: The ampulla is the swollen region at the base of a semicircular canal that contains the sensory receptors for rotation. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h3)

question: What causes the cupula to bend during head rotation?

options.A: Gravity pulling down on tiny calcium carbonate stones
options.B: Direct pressure from contracting neck muscles
options.C: The lagging movement of endolymph fluid against it
options.D: Changes in blood pressure within the inner ear

explanation: Inertia causes the endolymph fluid to move slower than the bony canal, pushing on the flexible cupula and bending the sensory hairs. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h3)

question: What are the tiny calcium carbonate crystals found in the otolith organs called?
explanation: Otoliths are microscopic crystals that add weight to the gelatinous membrane in the utricle and saccule. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h4)

question: A patient rides an elevator downward. Which structure primarily detects this downward linear movement?
explanation: The otolith organs, specifically the utricle and saccule, detect straight-line movements and gravitational forces like riding an elevator. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h4)

question: What is the tall, dominant hair on a vestibular receptor cell called?
explanation: The kinocilium is the single tallest hair in the bundle that determines whether the cell depolarizes or hyperpolarizes. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h5)

question: What happens inside a vestibular hair cell when its stereocilia bend toward the kinocilium?

options.A: Ion channels open and the cell depolarizes.
options.B: Potassium channels close and the cell dies.
options.C: Calcium crystals dissolve into the endolymph.
options.D: The cell releases stored digestive enzymes.

explanation: Bending toward the kinocilium stretches tip links, opening ion channels that let potassium in, resulting in cellular depolarization. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h5)

question: Which cranial nerve carries balance signals from the inner ear to the brain?
explanation: Cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve, transmits both hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the brainstem. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h6)

question: What is the primary function of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)?

options.A: To keep vision stable on an object during head movement
options.B: To focus the lens of the eye on distant objects
options.C: To adjust pupil size in response to bright sunlight
options.D: To control the blinking rate of both eyelids

explanation: The VOR coordinates eye movements opposite to head rotation so that visual focus remains fixed on a target. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h6)

question: Which sensory system detects body position through joint receptors and muscle stretch?
explanation: Proprioception involves specialized receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints that report body position and limb location to the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h7)

question: Why does reading a book inside a moving vehicle sometimes cause motion sickness?

options.A: Visual inputs override and shut down the cerebellum.
options.B: Eyes report no movement while the inner ear senses motion.
options.C: The inner ear fails to detect the motion of the vehicle.
options.D: Proprioceptive receptors in the feet are overstimulated.

explanation: Motion sickness happens when sensory inputs conflict, such as the eyes seeing a stationary book while the vestibular system feels motion. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h7)

question: What causes Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)?

options.A: Dislodged otolith crystals floating into a semicircular canal
options.B: A sudden drop in systemic arterial blood pressure
options.C: An acute bacterial infection of the middle ear space
options.D: Complete degeneration of the cochlear nerve fibers

explanation: BPPV happens when loose otolith crystals enter the semicircular canals, causing brief, intense spinning sensations with head movement. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h8)

question: What is the underlying physiological cause of Meniere's disease?

options.A: Degeneration of motor neurons in the spinal cord
options.B: Inflammation of the optic nerve affecting vision
options.C: An abnormal buildup of endolymph fluid in the inner ear
options.D: Complete blockage of the external auditory ear canal

explanation: Meniere's disease is characterized by an excessive accumulation of endolymphatic fluid, leading to vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T8#GNS211_U4_T8_h8)

question: What type of stimulus does the sense of smell detect?
explanation: Olfaction is a chemical sense that responds specifically to airborne chemical molecules entering the nasal cavity. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h1)

question: Why is the sense of smell so important for tasting food?

options.A: Taste buds on the tongue directly stimulate olfactory receptors
options.B: Saliva breaks down food chemicals into light waves for the nose
options.C: Odor molecules travel to the nasal cavity during chewing and swallowing
options.D: The stomach sends electrical signals to the olfactory bulb

explanation: As food is chewed, volatile molecules travel up through the nasopharynx to reach olfactory receptors, heavily shaping flavor. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h1)

question: Where is the smell-sensitive tissue located in the nasal cavity?
explanation: The olfactory epithelium sits high up on the roof of the nasal cavity, directly beneath the cribriform plate. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h2)

question: What is the special job of basal cells in the olfactory tissue?

options.A: They regulate body temperature inside the nasal passage
options.B: They send electrical signals directly to the temporal lobe
options.C: They secrete thick mucus to trap incoming dust particles
options.D: They divide to regenerate damaged olfactory receptor neurons

explanation: Basal cells act as stem cells that constantly replace worn-out or injured olfactory receptor neurons. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h2)

question: Which molecule acts as a second messenger to open ion channels when we smell something?
explanation: The activation of adenylate cyclase raises cyclic AMP levels, which opens sodium and calcium channels to depolarize the cell. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h3)

question: If a drug blocks adenylate cyclase in nose neurons, what happens?

options.A: Immediate destruction of all basal stem cells in the nose
options.B: Permanent physical damage to the cribriform plate
options.C: Inability to generate action potentials in response to smells
options.D: Excessive production of thick mucus in the nasal passages

explanation: Blocking adenylate cyclase halts the signaling cascade needed to open ion channels, preventing depolarization and smell perception. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h3)

question: Through which bone structure do smell nerve fibers pass to reach the brain?
explanation: The olfactory nerve fibers travel through the small holes of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h4)

question: What is the main job of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb?

options.A: They produce new stem cells to replace damaged olfactory neurons
options.B: They physically anchor the olfactory bulb to the frontal lobe
options.C: They secrete the protective mucus layer found in the nasal cavity
options.D: They serve as synaptic convergence points for specific receptor axons

explanation: Glomeruli organize incoming signals by collecting inputs from receptor cells expressing the same type of odorant receptor. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h4)

question: Which major brain relay station is skipped by smell nerve signals?
explanation: Unlike other special senses, olfaction projects directly to the cortex and limbic system without an initial relay in the thalamus. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h5)

question: Why do certain smells trigger emotional memories so quickly?

options.A: The thalamus filters out emotional data from all visual inputs
options.B: Olfactory receptor cells are actual extensions of the cerebral cortex
options.C: Olfactory pathways project directly to the limbic system and amygdala
options.D: Visual signals must travel slower because the eyes process light waves

explanation: Direct connections to limbic structures like the amygdala and hippocampus allow smells to trigger deep emotional and memory centers instantly. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h5)

question: What term describes getting used to a constant smell over time?
explanation: Olfactory adaptation is the fading of perceived odor intensity during prolonged continuous exposure. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h6)

question: Why is olfactory adaptation helpful for the human body?

options.A: It permanently destroys old receptor cells to make room for new ones
options.B: It stops volatile chemicals from reaching the delicate cribriform plate
options.C: It prevents sensory overload and keeps receptors alert to new smells
options.D: It directly stimulates the production of mucus in the nasal cavity

explanation: Adapting to constant background odors ensures the nervous system remains sensitive to sudden environmental changes or new hazards. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h6)

question: What medical term means a complete loss of the sense of smell?
explanation: Anosmia is the medical term for the total absence of the ability to detect odors. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h7)

question: A patient suffers a head injury that damages the cribriform plate. What symptom is expected?

options.A: Anosmia due to severed olfactory nerve fibers
options.B: Parosmia due to overactive basal cell regeneration
options.C: Hyposmia caused by chronic nasal polyp growth
options.D: Total loss of visual acuity from optic nerve damage

explanation: Fractures or shearing forces across the cribriform plate can easily sever the fine olfactory nerve filaments, leading to permanent anosmia. [learn more](GNS211_U4_T9#GNS211_U4_T9_h7)
